issue.title: [RFC]: Fast Start: keep the KV cache and prefix cache across engine restarts

repository.name: vllm
repository.description: A high-throughput and memory-efficient inference and serving engine for LLMs

issue.body:
> Review copy on the `hutm` fork. It has not been posted to the upstream project yet.

### Motivation.

Fast Start (`#54921`, `vllm preload` in `#56680`) lets a restarted engine skip loading its weights: a per-GPU daemon holds them and the new engine maps them. The engine still comes back with an empty KV cache, though. Every prompt it served before the restart is computed again, and that happens at the worst moment: right after a crash or a rolling restart, while traffic is coming back.

The daemon is already a process that outlives the engine on the same GPU. If it also held the engine's KV memory, the next engine could map the same bytes and keep serving from the old prefix cache. Nothing is copied, offloaded or recomputed.

That is what this RFC proposes, kept small for a first version:

- The KV cache and prefix cache survive an engine restart, including `kill -9`, as long as the `vllm preload` daemon keeps running.
- It is opt-in. Nothing changes for anyone who doesn't turn it on.
- One engine writes to a pool at a time.
- No orchestrator is needed: a plain `vllm serve` restarted by a shell script or by Kubernetes gets it.

Nothing upstream does this today. The Fast Start tracker (`#56049`) covers weights, autotune and parallelism. Offloading and connectors (`#19854`, LMCache, Mooncake, NIXL) copy KV to another tier and back. `#50265` recomputes unfinished requests inside a process that survived. Initialized snapshots (`#51360`) speed up startup but don't carry the KV of a process that crashed.

### Proposed Change.

#### How it works

1. **The daemon holds the KV memory as file descriptors.** With KV restore on, each worker allocates its KV cache as one shareable CUDA VMM allocation and passes its POSIX fd to its GPU's daemon. Holding the fd is enough to keep the memory alive after the engine exits. The daemon makes no CUDA calls for KV and never touches its contents.
2. **The open connection is the writer lease.** The worker keeps its session to the daemon open while it runs. When the engine dies, for any reason, the daemon sees EOF and releases the lease, but keeps the fds.
3. **The daemon keeps a directory of the prefix cache.** The scheduler streams its cached blocks to the daemon of worker 0:
   - **commit**: a block is sent only after the step that wrote it has finished. vLLM marks blocks as cached at schedule time, before the GPU writes them, so the commit waits until that step's output has been processed. This also holds with async scheduling.
   - **evict**: sent before a cached block can be reused, on the same ordered stream.

   So a crash never leaves a half-written block in the directory.
4. **The next engine maps the same memory and imports the directory.** A new engine with the same layout key re-attaches the pool, without zero-filling it, and imports the directory as cached, free blocks with `BlockPool.import_cached_blocks`. Its first request hits the old prefix cache.

#### User-facing API

Opt-in, through the existing loader config:

```bash
vllm preload --model MODEL                       # the daemon, as today
vllm serve MODEL --load-format ipc_cache \
  --model-loader-extra-config '{"kv_restore": true}'
```

Nothing else is needed. If the daemon is unreachable or busy, the engine logs a warning and starts with a normal KV cache.

To drop a retained pool (new in v1):

```bash
vllm preload --kv-drop [--force]   # talks to the running daemons; refused while an engine holds the lease, unless --force
```

Restarting the daemon also drops every pool.

#### Daemon protocol

These are new messages on the daemon's existing Unix socket. Each KV session runs on its own thread, so the daemon keeps serving weights.

| Message | From | Payload | Reply |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kv_attach` | worker | `key`, `nbytes`, `num_blocks` | `restore` (+ fd, `generation`, `size`), `fresh`, or `busy` |
| `kv_deposit` | worker, after `fresh` | `size`, `num_fds` + the fd (SCM_RIGHTS) | `ok` + `generation` |
| `kv_directory` | scheduler | directory key, the `generation` of every worker | `ok` + entries, or `busy` |
| `commit` | scheduler | `[(block_id, block_hash, num_tokens)]` | none (ordered stream) |
| `evict` | scheduler | `[block_id]` | none |
| `clear` | scheduler | (`reset_prefix_cache`) | none |
| `kv_probe` | anyone | — | pool size, block count, whether it's leased |
| `kv_drop` (new) | CLI | `force` | `ok` or `busy` |

The `kv_attach` and `kv_directory` connections stay open; their EOF ends the lease.

#### The layout key

A pool is reused only if everything that decides what its bytes mean is identical. The worker's key is a hash of:

- the model;
- the model dtype and the KV cache dtype;
- the resolved KV cache layout (`#51718`);
- the backing size and the number of blocks;
- every KV cache tensor (size and layers);
- every KV cache group (layers and spec).

The weights themselves are already checked by the daemon's `WeightCacheKey` before KV restore starts.

The directory has its own key: the block-hash seed (`NONE_HASH`), the block count and the hash block size. With TP, the directory is imported only if every worker re-attached its own previous pool. Each pool has a generation id, and the scheduler checks that all of them still match.

On a restart, the engine pins its block count to the held pool's, so the layout lines up by default.

#### Failure modes

| Case | What happens |
|---|---|
| Engine crashes (any signal, OOM, `kill -9`) | Lease released; pool and directory kept. Blocks not yet committed aren't in the directory, so they are never imported. |
| Layout key differs (new model, dtype, block count …) | The daemon drops the old pool and the engine starts fresh. A pool is never remapped under a different layout. |
| A second engine attaches while a writer is alive | `busy`: it runs with a normal, private KV cache and no restore. |
| Some TP worker got a fresh pool | Generations don't match, so the directory is discarded and nothing is imported. |
| Block-hash seed changed (xxhash without a fixed `PYTHONHASHSEED`) | The directory key differs, so nothing is imported. The default `sha256` uses a fixed seed. |
| Daemon dies or restarts | All pools are dropped; the next engine starts fresh. A running engine keeps its own mapping. |
| Engine shuts down gracefully | The pool is kept, because the next start is the point. Use `--kv-drop` to free it. |

#### Warmup on a restored cache

The V2 model runner's kernel warmup runs real scheduler steps that write KV blocks 1..N. On a restored cache, that overwrote prefix blocks before they were imported, and the outputs changed. v1 runs the warmup with block-table writes redirected to the null block (`preserve_serving_state`, as the elastic EP warmup already does). Without this, a restart corrupts the restored cache, so it is part of v1.

#### Engine changes

They are small and opt-in, and do nothing unless KV restore is on:

- **KV backing allocation.** `allocate_kv_cache` takes the backing buffer from the caller instead of allocating and zero-filling one. We'd like to use the `allocate=` callback from `#56492` rather than add a second hook, and add `export_fd`/`import_fd` to its VMM driver.
- **BlockPool hooks.** These are callbacks for blocks cached and evicted, and for the step boundaries `on_step_scheduled(output)` / `on_step_output_processed(output)`. The scheduler calls them. A `KVRestoreBlockPool` subclass uses them and is selected automatically.
- **`BlockPool.import_cached_blocks(block_hashes, block_ids)`.** This registers existing KV as normal cached blocks.
- **`request_memory(..., reclaimable_memory=)`.** The pool the daemon holds for this engine counts as free in the startup memory check.
- **The warmup change above.**

#### Why not KV events?

KV events (`BlockStored` / `BlockRemoved`, plus `#50134` snapshots) look close, but they don't fit:

- They fire when a block is scheduled, before the GPU writes it.
- They carry hashes, not block ids.
- They go out over pub/sub, which may drop messages.

The directory needs "commit after the write, evict before the reuse" over one ordered stream.

#### How this compares with KV connectors, LMCache, offloading

These are complementary.

| | Offloading / LMCache / Mooncake / NIXL | KV restore v1 |
|---|---|---|
| Where KV lives across a restart | CPU, disk or a remote store | The same GPU memory, unchanged |
| Cost to get it back | A copy back per hit, after the engine is up | None: the memory is mapped at startup |
| After a crash | Only what was stored before the crash | Everything committed before the crash |
| Recompute | None for stored blocks, but the copy-back costs time | None for committed blocks |
| Scope | Across GPUs and nodes; capacity beyond HBM | Same GPU only; capacity is the HBM pool |

Why it's complementary:

- **No copy.** The restored engine starts with a warm prefix cache, and nothing is moved.
- **Instant restore after a crash.** It doesn't depend on a store being up or on what was offloaded before the crash.
- **It works with any connector setup.** The connector still sees ordinary blocks and an ordinary KV buffer, so an offload tier can sit behind a restored cache.

Where it's not a fit:

- Moving KV to another GPU or node (use a connector).
- Capacity beyond HBM.
- Sleep mode (refused in v1).
- A daemon that restarts together with the engine.
- Several engines sharing one GPU's KV at once.

#### Results

Setup:

- Qwen3-0.6B on one B200, 2 GiB KV pool, CUDA graphs on.
- `vllm preload --weight-cache-transport vmm_fd` next to `vllm serve --load-format ipc_cache` with `kv_restore`.
- Prompts of 1258 tokens sharing a 1248-token prefix.
- The server's whole process group was SIGKILLed while a streaming request was decoding, then a new `vllm serve` was started on the same daemon.

Two back-to-back runs:

| | Disk-loaded `vllm serve` | `vllm serve` restarted on the daemon |
|---|---|---|
| Time to `/health` | 27.6–27.8 s | 27.0–27.2 s |
| Model loaded by the engine | 1.12 GiB | 0 GiB (weights mapped) |
| Cached tokens, first request | 0 of 1258 | **1248 of 1258** |

- The restarted server imported 86 blocks. The killed stream's partial block was not adopted.
- Greedy outputs matched the pre-crash server's and a disk-loaded server's.

To be clear about time to ready: it barely moves. Most of the 27 s is process start, the API server, engine init and CUDA graph capture, which every new process repeats. Reading a 0.6B checkpoint is a fraction of a second. The gain is:

- a warm prefix cache on the first request, instead of recomputing every prompt;
- no weight reload, which matters more as the checkpoint grows.

Startup cost is a separate problem (snapshots, `#51360`; graph caching).

#### Limits in v1

- Opt-in, and only with `--load-format ipc_cache` and a running daemon.
- Not compatible with sleep mode, or with `--enable-extensible-kv-cache` (`#56492`) until we agree how they compose.
- A retained pool keeps its GPU memory after the engine exits, until a matching engine attaches, the pool is dropped, or the daemon stops. Operators doing rolling updates with a *different* config should drop it first. A different key drops it on attach anyway.
- Blocks with several cache-group hashes (overlaid hybrid groups) restore only their primary hash.
- Tested end to end at TP1 only. TP is covered by unit tests (per-worker generations).

#### Future work: warm standby (phase 2)

A restart still pays for process start and graph capture: about 27 s here, more on large models. A warm standby, already loaded and captured on the same GPU and sharing the daemon's weights and the writer's KV pool, could take over within milliseconds of a crash. We have this working on top of v1; promotion took about 3 ms in our tests.

It needs more API: a standby role, a promote call, keeping a booting standby from writing into the live pool, and fencing the old writer's in-flight blocks. That deserves its own discussion, and it should plug into the fault-tolerance control plane (`#44428`, `#46370`) rather than add a new one. We'll post it as a follow-up once v1 is settled.

#### PR plan

1. VMM fd export/import for KV allocations. This builds on `#56492`'s VMM driver if that lands first.
2. Engine hooks: backing allocation, BlockPool callbacks and step boundaries, `import_cached_blocks`, `reclaimable_memory`.
3. KV restore in the weight cache daemon, the `kv_drop` command, and the warmup change, with unit tests and one restart e2e test (`kill -9` mid-decode; cached tokens > 0; greedy outputs equal to before the crash and to a disk load).

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@liusy58 @Isotr0py @njhill @heheda12345 @WoosukKwon @orozery

### Any Other Things.

Questions we'd like input on:

- Should KV restore stay in `--model-loader-extra-config`, or become its own flag (e.g. `--kv-restore`)?
- Is `#56492`'s `allocate=` callback the right place to plug in the backing buffer? Should its VMM driver grow `export_fd`/`import_fd`, or should KV restore keep its own small wrapper?
- Should the BlockPool callbacks be methods on a subclass, as proposed, or a listener object?
- Should graceful shutdown keep the pool (proposed) or drop it by default?
- Where should `kv_drop` live: a `vllm preload` subcommand or flag that talks to the running daemons (proposed), or an HTTP route next to the daemon's `/health` (`#58552`)?

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
